text: Last lesson's pilot proved something in one domain, in one fixed window. A roadmap is what turns that single proof point into an organization-wide program — sequenced in phases, not repeated everywhere at once.

A realistic roadmap has roughly five phases. Days zero to thirty: discovery — goals, stakeholders, pain points. Days thirty-one to sixty: foundation — first owners, first policies, first catalog entries. Days sixty-one to ninety: the pilot itself, running inside the roadmap. Months three to six: expand to two or three more domains. Months six to twelve: scale into business as usual.

A roadmap that's just colored boxes on a timeline is decoration, not a plan. Every phase needs a named owner for that phase's work, a defined output — an artifact or capability that now exists — and a measurable milestone anyone can check against reality.

Roadmaps fail quietly two ways: marching forward on schedule even when a phase's milestone wasn't actually hit, or treating the whole thing as aspirational — a wall poster nobody checks. Revisit it at the end of every phase and adjust the next one based on what actually happened.

Discovery, foundation, pilot, expand, scale — each phase owned, defined, and measured. That's a roadmap built to survive contact with reality. Next up: putting all of this into language the rest of the business will actually listen to.
